candidates.name: Pyramid of Gaius Cestius
candidates.content: A tomb for the wealthy Gaius Cestius, who died in 12 BC. Admission to the monument only by guided tours on specific dates (2nd and 4th Saturday every month, and in combination with a ticket to the Museum of Via Ostiense also on th

candidates.name: Museum of Via Ostiense
candidates.content: This is a small museum housed inside Porta San Paolo, which records the importance to Rome of the road that connected it to the harbour at Ostia. There are models of old Ostia and Trajan's harbour.

candidates.name: Trajan's Markets
candidates.content: On the other side of the Via dei Fori Imperiali to the Roman Forum. Well-preserved market area that doubled as a way of stopping the Quirinal Hill from collapsing. Below in the Forum is Trajan's Column, built in 113 with reliefs d

candidates.name: Palazzo Doria Pamphilj
candidates.content: Good collection of Renaissance and Baroque art, including by Velasquez, Titian, Raphael, and Bernini, all owned by the Doria Pamphilj family. Excellent audio guides really bring the paintings to life.

candidates.name: Museo della Liberazione
candidates.content: This small museum records the liberation of Rome from German occupation during the Second World War. During the occupation the building was used as a prison. Stair lifts and chair lifts available for wheelchair users (call ahead).

candidates.name: Palazzo Barberini
candidates.price: €5, several discounts available. Free entrance for people under 18 and over 65
candidates.content: This remarkable building, designed partly by Bernini, houses the National Gallery of Ancient Art, and includes some famous paintings by Filippo Lippi and Caravaggio, as well as Raphael's "La Fornarina".

candidates.name: Casina delle Civette
candidates.hours: 09:00-16:00 in winter and to 19:00 in summer
candidates.content: This strange-looking, but delightful, building has undergone several transformations since its original construction as a rustic hideaway from the main villa in the park. It underwent a significant redesign in the early 1900s and

candidates.name: The Spanish Steps
candidates.content: A truly monumental stairway of 135 steps (similar to climbing eight flights of stairs), built with French funds between 1721 and 1725 in order to link the Bourbon Spanish embassy to the Holy See (still located in the piazza below)

candidates.name: Villa Borghese
candidates.hours: Tue-Sun 08:30-19:30 (mandatory exit at the end of allotted 2-hour slot, ticket office closes at 18:30)
candidates.content: Borghese Gallery and Museum is a lovely display in a beautiful villa setting, which concentrates on the quality rather than the size of its collection. There are some very notable works by Antonio Canova and Gian Lorenzo Bernini h

candidates.name: Villa Giulia National Gallery
candidates.price: Full €8, concessions for students and pensioners
candidates.content: The most extensive collection of Etruscan art and artifacts anywhere. Fantastic collection and well worth the admission charge. A difficult museum to find, but a lovely display in a beautiful villa setting.

candidates.name: Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Moderna (GNAM)
candidates.alt: the National Gallery of Modern Art
candidates.content: An underrated way to see fantastic art made after the Renaissance. Mainly Italian artists, notably De Chirico, but Cézanne, Degas, Kandinsky, Man Ray, Modigliani, Monet, Pollock and Van Gogh are also represented.

candidates.name: MACRO
candidates.hours: Tue-Sun 10:30-19:00 (last admission 1 hour before closing), Mon closed
candidates.content: Rome's museum of contemporary art, housed in a former industrial complex. Rotating exhibitions, each one usually lasting about 4 months. The MACRO Testaccio exhibition space is located in Aventino-Testaccio.

candidates.name: The Pantheon
candidates.alt: Basilica of St. Mary and the Martyrs
candidates.hours: Mon-Sat 08:00-19:30, Sun 09:00-18:00, public holidays 09:00-13:00, closed Jan 1, May 1, Dec 25
candidates.content: It was built in 27 BCE, by Augustus' right hand man Marcus Agrippa, and later remodeled by the Emperor Hadrian (AD 125-128). This ancient temple was built as a temple to all the gods of the Roman state but has served as a Christia

candidates.name: Palazzo Altemps
candidates.alt: Branch of the Roman National Museum
candidates.price: €15 (less for EU citizens of ages 18-24) gives admission to this and the three other National Museums of Rome
candidates.content: Simple and elegant lines make up this building, whose construction began in 1480 for Count Girolamo Riario, nephew of Papa Sisto IV, and was taken up by architect Martino Longhi for the new owner, Cardinal Marco Sittico Altemps. T

candidates.name: Crypta Balbi
candidates.alt: branch of the National Museum of Rome (Museo Nazionale Romano)
candidates.price: €10 adult, €6.50 EU citizens age 18-24 for access to all four National Museum of Rome sites
candidates.content: This museum is built on top of the excavation site of the Balbi Crypt, a building from the first century A.D. which underwent considerable modifications in the following centuries. Through the building's history, the museum gives

candidates.name: Museum of the Walls
candidates.content: Porta San Sebastiano is a gate in the amazingly well-preserved Aurelian Walls. Inside and upstairs is a museum dedicated to the construction of the walls and their recent restoration. You can take a walk along the top of the walls

candidates.name: The Catacombs of San Domitilla
candidates.content: The Catacombs of Domitilla are considered to be the best preserved of all Roman catacombs. They are the only ones still to contain bones. Domitilla also has a subterranean basilica, much of which was reconstructed in 1870.

candidates.name: Basilica and catacombs of San Sebastiano
candidates.content: The first basilica was constructed in the 4th century and dedicated to San Sebastian, a martyr of the 3rd century. Sebastian's remains were transferred to St. Peter's in 826, prior to a Saracen assault when the church was destroye

candidates.name: Villa dei Quintilii
candidates.price: A €5 ticket gives admission to the villa, to Santa Maria Nova, and to Cecilia Metella
candidates.hours: Tue-Sun 09:00-19:00 or sunset, whichever is earlier
candidates.content: This impressive villa covers 23 hectares. It can be accessed from the Via Appia Nuova (Bus 118) or through Via Appia Antica 251. Parts can be seen from the Appian Way at around the 5th mile just after No 251. The villa was built b

candidates.name: Centrale Montemartini Museum
candidates.price: €4.50 plus extra fees for special exhibits
candidates.content: This delightful museum provides an interesting juxtaposition between the buildings and equipment of Rome's first electricity generating plant and the exhibits, which are mainly from excavations of Roman sites. A combined ticket wi

candidates.name: Museum of Rome in Trastevere
candidates.hours: Tue-Sun 10:00-20:00, Mon closed. Last admission 1h before closing
candidates.content: Permanent collection features paintings and drawings of Rome between the 18th and 20th centuries together with a fascinating black and white photo exhibition of Rome from 1950-80. Also offers rotating exhibitions, usually of the w

candidates.name: St. Peter's Basilica
candidates.hours: Apr-Sep: 07:00-19:00, Oct-Mar: 07:00-18:00. Closed on Wed mornings for papal audiences and may be closed for other occasions.
candidates.content: The centre of the Catholic world, this magnificent basilica with its Michelangelo-designed dome has an awe-inspiring interior. This place is huge, but everything is in such proportion that the scale escapes you. However, contrary

candidates.name: St. Peter's Square
candidates.content: Most of the Piazza di San Pietro is actually an oval. There is a small, almost rectangular section immediately in front of the St Peter's and an opening to the Via della Conciliazione opposite the basilica.

candidates.name: The Vatican Museum
candidates.price: €16 adults, €8 concessions. Additional €4 booking fee per ticket if booked online in advance. As of 2025, the number of visitors is extremely high and often the only tickets available to book online include a guided tour - €40 per person.
candidates.hours: Mon-Sat 09:00-18:00 (ticket office closes at 16:00), Sun closed (except last Sun of the month, when it is free, crowded, and open 09:00-14:00 with the last admission at 12:30). The museum is closed for holidays on Jan 1 and 6, Feb 11 and 22, Mar 19 and 28, Jun 29, Aug 15, Nov 1, and Dec 8 and 26
candidates.content: One of the greatest art galleries in the world, the museum is most famous for its spiral staircase, the Raphael Rooms and the exquisitely decorated Sistine Chapel famous for Michelangelo's frescoes.

candidates.name: Castel Sant'Angelo
candidates.content: Perhaps the most fascinating building in Rome. The core of the structure began life as the mausoleum of Emperor Hadrian, built between 135 and 139 AD. Subsequent strongholds built on top of the mausoleum were in turn incorporated

candidates.name: Parco Savello
candidates.content: Parco Savello is the name of the grounds and orange grove next to the Santa Sabina church at the top of the Aventino and also where you have one of the best views of the city. Families gather here to sit under the dozens of orange

candidates.name: Basilica of Santa Sabina
candidates.content: A 5th-century basilica, simply and attractively decorated. The wooden door, of which 18 carved panels of scenes from the Bible survive, is believed to date from the church's construction.

candidates.name: Santa Maria in Cosmedin
candidates.content: A medieval church dating from the 6th century and home to the Bocca della Verità (Mouth of Truth). The Bocca della Verità at the entrance to the church is thought to be a 1st-century manhole cover. It is believed that if you put y

candidates.name: Festa dell'Unità
candidates.content: This is a traditional popular festival, once organised by the Italian Communist Party to promote its official newspaper l'Unità ("Unity"), and nowadays kept by the Democratic Party. Held annually in mid-June in Rome's archaeologic

candidates.name: Estate Romana Festival
candidates.content: From late June through early September offers various musical events of jazz, rock, and classical music, and film, sport, theater and children’s fun.

candidates.name: Auditorium Parco della Musica
candidates.content: The Auditorium at Parco della Musica is a large complex on the north side of Rome, built on a site that was part of the 1960 Olympic area. It is composed of three separate halls whose shapes are inspired by musical instruments. Th

candidates.name: Piazza S. Maria in Trastevere
candidates.content: Beautiful place to hang around and watch people going by, as well as the many buskers usually found in the square. Join the students sitting on the steps of the fountain or, if you can afford it, have a drink or meal at one of the

candidates.name: Palazzo delle Esposizioni
candidates.price: €12.50; reductions €10. You can purchase a discounted, combined ticket for the Palazzo and the Scuderie.
candidates.content: Rotating exhibitions, usually three at one time. Exhibition descriptions normally provided in both Italian and English. Avoid Sunday morning, when the Romans go, as queues to get in can be long.

candidates.name: Opera at Caracalla
candidates.content: If you are in Rome during summertime don’t miss the chance to experience a lyric opera in the truly unique setting of the Caracalla Baths. The 2009 program included Tosca, Carmen and Midsummer Night’s Dream. Performances start at

candidates.name: Scuderie del Quirinale
candidates.content: Former stables of the Quirinal Palace, now an exhibition centre that usually hosts some excellent art shows.

candidates.name: Testaccio Market
candidates.content: Great place to see the wide range of fresh produce available in Italy. Fish and flower stalls as well. Stock up here for picnics to sustain you while sightseeing.

candidates.name: White Night (Notte Bianca)
candidates.content: In early to mid-September, various events until dawn, plus shops and restaurants, museums stay open while the Roman Notte Bianca stages music, dance and theater events. Expect enormous crowds; buses and trams will be packed to the

candidates.name: Big Mama
candidates.hours: Shows normally begin around 22:00 but check Press for details
candidates.content: Rome’s original "House of the Blues". Has been going strong for 25 years. Italian and international artists, with blues and jazz concerts.

candidates.name: Get lost in Trastevere
candidates.content: The cobbled streets are narrow and winding and random but losing your way will lead you to places you might not otherwise find. Note that the cobblestone streets (locally called sampietrini) are being paved elsewhere in Rome as th

candidates.name: Bike
candidates.content: Rent a bike and explore the many remains of the Appian Way park area.

candidates.name: Antico Caffe Greco
candidates.content: In March 2026, it is closed due to a rent dispute. Ancient and famous coffee bar, with walls lined with art work. Worth a quick look even if you find the prices a bit excessive.

candidates.name: Babington's Tea Rooms
candidates.content: situated right next to the base of the Spanish Steps, a veritable tourist trap. The cheapest pot of tea is €8. It opened in 1896 in order to fortify homesick English tourists, once famous as a tranquil English haven in a Latin oce

candidates.name: L'Oasi della Birra
candidates.content: In a basement underneath a wine shop opposite Testaccio market, L’Oasi della Birra is a bar with a wide selection of beers from Italy and around the world on offer, as well as some interesting food to go with the beer. The selecti

candidates.name: Shamrock
candidates.content: If touring the ancient sites of Rome is wearing you out and you're dying for an afternoon beer, head to this quiet Irish pub in a little laneway just off the right side of bottom of Via Cavour, which is a busy street that is more

candidates.name: Enoteca Cavour
candidates.content: Great wine bar with a selection of wines by the glass and hundreds of bottles to choose from. Wooden decor, paper tablecloths and wines stored overhead. Good food too.

candidates.name: Harrys Bar
candidates.content: You can't visit Via Veneto and not go to Harrys Bar, forever associated with Fellinis' La Dolce Vita. Harrys is now a swanky upmarket {read expensive} bar/eatery where celebs can still be spotted. A piano bar. Sometimes guest arti

candidates.name: The Drunken Ship
candidates.content: Western bar. Nice for a quiet afternoon drink but are usually quite noisy at night, with specials most nights to encourage business. Girls are encouraged to have fun by lying on the bar and allowing guys to drink shots off their c

candidates.name: Baccanale
candidates.content: A small bar with a great range of drinks, friendly staff and a manic display of cocktail making later on in the evening. There are several TV screens showing major sporting events. Probably the best bar in the world considering it

candidates.name: Be.Re
candidates.content: Good selection of craft beers, many on tap. If you're a beer lover, it's definitely worth going. Some snacks too, try some Trapizzino (triangular filled pizza).

candidates.name: Fiddler’s Elbow
candidates.content: The oldest Irish pub.

candidates.name: Druid’s Rock Pub
candidates.content: The sister pub of the Druid’s Den.

candidates.name: Babette caffe-ristorante
candidates.content: Lovely lunch buffet. Everything fresh out of the kitchen. Much more expensive on weekends. Always best to reserve. A nice way to sample lots of different Italian foods without having to order an antipasti, primi, secondi, etc.

candidates.name: Cafè Cafè
candidates.content: Cozy and quite cheap, this tea room is very close to the Colosseo, and it's ideal to have nice meeting with friends or a more intimate date. Very good sweets and tea, the choice is also good. Open all day and after dinner.

candidates.name: Dagnino Tea Room, Galleria
candidates.content: If you haven't tried a "Cannolo" or a "Cassatina" then get one here, they are simply great. Don't sit at the tables (it's pretty expensive) just take them away. Good pastries too.

candidates.name: Trattoria Pizzeria Luzzi
candidates.price: Antipasti: €0.50-12.00; primi piatti: €7.00-10.00; secondi piatti: €6.00-15.00; contorni: €3.00-7.00; dolci: €4.00-5.00; pizza and focaccia: €5.50-9.00
candidates.content: Tasty food, including particularly Roman dishes like pasta alla carbonara, trippa alla romana, carciofi alla giudia and coda alla vaccinara. Popular with Italians and foreigners alike, and strikingly affordable considering how clo

candidates.name: Aquila Nera, Ristorante Pizzeria
candidates.price: €25-35 for dinner including wine and bottled water
candidates.content: A street side restaurant with excellent food, attentive service and warm atmosphere. Eat outside or inside, depending on the weather. Try the fish fillet baked in potato which should please anyone who likes fish - it is excellent.

candidates.name: Trattoria Zampagna
candidates.content: Good Roman fare. One of the owners can speak English so that's helpful. Many interesting varieties of pasta along with traditional main courses such as ox tail. The owner has been known to take the time to introduce each of the di

candidates.name: Ai Bozzi
candidates.content: Italian restaurant with excellent food and professional service. Traditional dishes as well innovative variations (try the fettuccine with artichokes and guanciale). Pizza is also served in the evening. Lovely outside terrace over

candidates.name: Pizzeria La Boccaccia
candidates.content: Great little pizzeria run by 2 friendly Neapolitan brothers. You can get a big slice and a huge ice cold beer for €5. The place gets full of locals. That should tell you everything. get there quite early as in the evening they hav

candidates.name: Taverna Cestia
candidates.content: Excellent traditional Roman restaurant. The waiters do not speak much English. They have a good selection of seafood, and the seafood spaghetti is great.

candidates.name: Est! Est! Est!!!
candidates.content: The chefs here make a relatively small but amazingly good pizza. The calzone, one of their specialities, is excellent too. The staff speak English, and this is one of the few places where there are both plenty of tourists and very

candidates.name: Da Armando
candidates.content: A traditional Roman osteria with traditional Roman dishes as well as pizza. Lots of choice for both food and wine. Delicious homemade pasta. Prices are very reasonable and only few tourists.

candidates.name: Fiaschetteria Beltramme da Cesaretto
candidates.hours: Open for lunch and dinner. Closed Sun
candidates.content: Outdoor seating available. Cash only. Walls lined with interesting art and at least one communal table. Small, traditional menu but the best dishes are the pastas and the simple bresaola, rughetta and parmigiano plate. Recommended

candidates.name: Pizzeria da Baffetto
candidates.content: Old-fashioned, family feel pizzeria near Piazza Navona and the Pantheon, unarguably serving some of the best pizzas in Rome. Usually crowded but well-worth the occasional queuing.

candidates.name: Alice
candidates.content: Part of an Italian chain serving pizza al taglio (square pieces to be eaten by hand), dozens of pizzas to choose from.

candidates.name: Forno di Campo de' Fiori
candidates.content: A traditional bread shop that makes one of the best kinds of pizza bread in Rome. With your back to the Giordano Bruno statue in the middle of the square, the Forno is at the bottom of the square to the left. Good place to have lu

candidates.name: Mercato Esquilino
candidates.content: An indoor market of ancient provenance that has moved from its longtime outdoor home all the way round the outside of Piazza Vittorio; it is still only a couple of blocks east of the piazza. The mercato is divided into a food sect

candidates.name: Porta Portese
candidates.content: On Sunday mornings there is a huge flea market. It extends from Porta Portese to Viale di Trastevere.

december.text: There are two lines that cross at Termini station: line runs northwest past the Vatican and southeast, and line runs southwest past the Colosseum and northeast in one direction, but also splits at the "Bologna" station to go due north until Jonio. Line runs from Monte Compatri/Pantano in the eastern suburbs through San

South of the Colosseum are the Baths of Caracalla (Aventino-Testaccio). You can then head South-East on the old Appian Way, passing through a stretch of very well-preserved city wall. For the adventurous, continuing along the Appian Way (Rome/South) will bring you to a whole host of Roman ruins, including the Circus of

Main shopping areas include Via del Corso, Via Condotti, and the surrounding streets. The finest designer stores are around Via Condotti, whilst Via del Corso has more affordable clothing, and Via Cola di Rienzo, and the surroundings of Via del Tritone, Campo de'Fiori, and Pantheon are the places to go for cheaper item

Far from the centre there are some other good places. The Palacavicchi in a small suburban town called Ciampino is a multi-dance room area where they play different kinds of music, mostly Latin American. You definitely need to get a cab to get there and it won't cost less than €20. South of Ciampino Airport there is Th

Piazza del Popolo: This is the largest square in Rome. It sometimes hosts pop concerts and is the focal point for Rome's New Year's Eve celebrations. The twin churches Santa Maria dei Miracoli (1681) and Santa Maria in Montesanto (1679) used to provide a clear welcome to Rome for those coming from

Piazza di Spagna: The Piazza di Spagna (Spanish Square) is the most famous square in Rome. For a very long time it was the meeting point of all foreigners coming to Rome. In the 17th century it was the residence of the Spanish Ambassador to the Holy See. The area around the residence was Spanish t

Passetto di Borgo: Pope Nicholas III connected Castel Sant'Angelo to St. Peter's by a covered fortified corridor called the Passetto di Borgo.
